Project overview

Tetrisly is a commercial Design System built as a standalone product — a component library for Figma with over 300 accessible, customisable components, sold as an annual subscription.

This was the product and project I spent the most time with and that involved the most comprehensive activities — spanning UX research, user flow analysis, component documentation, and UX writing. The most extensive and multifaceted project in my portfolio.

01Understanding 02Research 03Analysis 04Design 05Outcome
01 — Understanding

Product
Definition

Tetrisly is a Design System sold as a commercial product — a Figma component library with over 300 carefully selected, accessible, and customisable components, available as an annual subscription ($99/year). My involvement covered the full product lifecycle: from understanding how users experience the product, through research and analysis, to designing documentation and improving the user journey.

In addition to the main tasks described below, I was responsible for content on the website and other materials (UX writing based on Plain Language principles), the Getting Started section of the tool, and landing page consultations.

Product
DS as a product

A universal, commercial Design System — not built for one client, but sold to designers and teams worldwide. Available as a free version (Figma) and a paid Pro tier.

Business goal
Grow & retain users

Improve the experience from first contact with the product all the way through to daily usage — reducing friction in onboarding, purchasing, and keeping up with updates.

My scope
End-to-end involvement
  • UX research — interviews, synthesis, workshop
  • User flow analysis & problem mapping
  • Component documentation subpages
  • UX writing — Getting Started, emails, website
02 — Research

User & Market
Insights

I conducted two rounds of individual interviews — Q3 and Q4 2023 — with potential users of Tetrisly: designers, DS specialists, and teams at various stages of product development. The research aimed to understand how people discover, evaluate, and use a commercial Design System.

The interviews were planned, conducted, tagged, and synthesised in Dovetail. Results were presented to the whole team in a structured summary presentation.

Research process
5-stage methodology
  • Stage 1 — Team brainstorm workshop: "What don't we know?" — mapping knowledge gaps
  • Stage 2 — Defining research questions and target groups
  • Stage 3 — Writing research scenarios, conducting individual interviews (Q3 + Q4 2023)
  • Stage 4 — Tagging & synthesis in Dovetail repository
  • Stage 5 — Presenting findings and building strategy based on results
Who we talked to
Research participants
  • DS Specialists (internal and external)
  • Designers using Design Systems in teams
  • Frontend developers collaborating with designers
  • 5 designers + 3 specialists per round
  • Interviews conducted in Q3 2023 and Q4 2023
Stage 1 — Team brainstorm workshop: mapping what we don't know
Stage 3 — Research scenarios and interview structure
Stage 4 — Dovetail repository with tagged interview data
Stage 5 — Research results presented to the team (Q4 2023 summary)
03 — Analysis

Synthesis &
Decisions

I analysed the full User Flow — from pre-purchase research through installation, first use, daily usage, and updating. The main aim was to focus on the process the user goes through and find the problems they encounter. Based on this analysis, I led a workshop where the team discussed and identified opportunities to solve those problems.

User flow stages
Full journey mapping
  • Pre-purchase — research, evaluating options, scrolling LP
  • Purchasing — pricing page, buy CTA, email flow
  • Installing — downloading, importing to Figma, enabling library
  • First use — Getting Started, publishing library, what's next
  • Usage — working with components, plugin, tracking
  • Updating — library update issues, mailing, tutorial currency
Key problems found
Pain points identified
  • Getting Started section was outdated and not linked from Figma file at the right moment
  • No analytics tracking on key user actions (downloads, plugin usage)
  • Library update process was confusing — no clear guide or notification
  • Tutorial was not current and not included in documentation
  • Thank you page after purchase was a missed opportunity for onboarding
  • Broken links in the Figma file (React, plugin references)
Key insight from analysis

"The gap between downloading Tetrisly and actually using it successfully was the biggest friction point — users were left to figure out the first steps on their own."

04 — Design

Design
Process

Based on the research findings and user flow analysis, I worked on two main design areas: the component documentation subpages and the Getting Started experience. The documentation subpages describe individual components — their key features, variants, anatomy, best practices, and content guidelines — in a structure that is easily repeatable, consistent with other subpages, and implementable in Docusaurus.

Documentation subpages
Component pages
  • Consistent structure across all component pages
  • Key features, variants, anatomy, behaviour
  • Best practices — do's and don'ts
  • Content guidelines for UX writing
  • Designed to be easily repeatable and implementable in Docusaurus
  • Collaboration: PM, UI Designer, Graphic Designer, Frontend & Backend Dev, Marketing
UX Writing & onboarding
Getting Started & content
  • Rewrote the Getting Started section of the Figma file — based on Plain Language principles
  • New email sequences for post-purchase and post-download users
  • Website content consultations and copy improvements
  • Landing page consultations
  • Updated Thank you page to better guide users to next steps
Component documentation pages — Button, Text Input, Tabs, Radio Button, Badge — consistent structure across all components
05 — Outcome

Result

The research findings directly influenced the product roadmap — from improving the onboarding flow and Getting Started content, to launching new email sequences and updating the Thank you page. The component documentation subpages are live on the Tetrisly documentation site, providing a consistent and comprehensive reference for every component in the library.

Live product. Research-driven improvements.

The Tetrisly component documentation is live and available at tetrisly.com. Research findings from Q3 and Q4 2023 drove concrete product changes: updated Getting Started, new email sequences, improved onboarding flow, and fixed user journey gaps identified in the user flow analysis.
